disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, through learning of events to close others, or repeated exposure to aversive details. It is characterized by persistent re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of trauma-related cues, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity lasting more than one month and causing significant distress or functional impairment. The course can be acute or chronic, with onset soon after the trauma or delayed, and it often fluctuates in intensity over time in response to reminders and ongoing stress. It is distinguished from other disorders such as depression or generalized anxiety by the clear temporal relationship to a qualifying traumatic event and the central role of trauma-linked re-experiencing and avoidance phenomena.

narrative.personality: Jacqueline is a pragmatic, detail-focused tradesperson who prides herself on meticulous planning, hands-on mentoring, and a down-to-earth appreciation for nature, home cooking, and church community life.
narrative.stressor: About fourteen months ago, Jacqueline was working with her crew on a commercial renovation when a section of unsecured ceiling grid and drywall collapsed, pinning her and a younger apprentice beneath heavy debris until firefighters extricated them. She remained conscious throughout, convinced she was going to die as she struggled to breathe under the weight and listened to her apprentice screaming nearby, and she later learned in the hospital that the apprentice had suffered life-threatening injuries. After being discharged with multiple fractures and soft-tissue injuries, she initially threw herself into managing her recovery plan and paperwork, but over the following months she became increasingly unable to return to job sites or even enter hardware stores without intense distress, straining her role as a foreman and mentor and leaving her husband to shoulder more financial and emotional burdens. As the year wore on and she found herself withdrawing from her gardening, church volunteering, and family interactions while taking growing risks on her snowmobile and on icy roads, her pastor and husband urged her to see a psychiatrist when she admitted that she felt numb and disconnected from any sense of joy or love in her life.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like I just can’t feel happy or loving toward anyone anymore, no matter what I do.

narrative.personality: Kimberly is a quietly analytical, highly organized woman who enjoys solitary intellectual hobbies and gently mentoring others, while keeping her daily routines predictable and structured.
narrative.stressor: A little over a year ago, Kimberly’s husband of more than five decades was killed when a drunk driver struck their car head-on as they were returning from a small-town book club meeting; she survived with minor physical injuries but watched emergency responders work unsuccessfully to resuscitate him at the scene. In the months that followed, she tried to cope by meticulously handling the estate, finances, and funeral arrangements, telling herself that staying busy and keeping her routines would help her move forward. However, her usual pleasures—reading mysteries late into the night, gardening, bird watching, and participating in her book club—gradually fell away as each reminded her of moments shared with her husband or of the night of the accident, leading her to isolate more at home and reduce her volunteer work and advisory role. When a younger colleague she was mentoring and a fellow library volunteer both commented that she no longer seemed interested in anything and had stopped showing up to activities she once organized, she reluctantly agreed to see a psychiatrist after realizing she could not bring herself to re-engage with the hobbies and social circles that used to anchor her days.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve lost interest in all the things I used to enjoy and just can’t seem to care about them anymore.

narrative.personality: Silvia is a disciplined, intellectually curious teacher who channels her love of data, art, and careful planning into highly structured yet creative lessons and solitary, detail-oriented hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About thirteen months ago, Silvia was supervising an after-school STEM club when a former student entered the building with a firearm and opened fire in the hallway outside her classroom; she ushered several students into a storage area and barricaded the door while hearing shots, screams, and then a prolonged standoff until police evacuated them. Although she and her club members were physically unharmed, two students from her physics class were killed and another was critically injured, and she later spent hours in the gymnasium with terrified families waiting to learn who had survived. Initially, Silvia coped by throwing herself into organizing memorial projects and advocating for safety reforms, but over the subsequent months she found it increasingly difficult to be in the school building, to look at seating charts, or to prepare the kinds of inquiry-based projects she once loved, as everything seemed to bring the event back into sharp focus and left her exhausted and on edge. After a year of mounting strain, frequent absences, and a noticeable drop in her once-exemplary performance, her principal and spouse encouraged her to seek psychiatric help when she admitted that vivid, unwanted recollections of the shooting kept forcing their way into her mind during class and at home, undermining both her work and her quiet hobbies like painting and model rocketry.
narrative.chief_complaint: I keep getting these unwanted, vivid memories of the school shooting that pop into my head no matter what I’m doing.
